lesson.title: One Big Union: The Rise and Fall of the Knights of Labor
lesson.summary: The Knights of Labor grew from a secret society of Philadelphia garment cutters into the first mass labor organization in American history, welcoming nearly every kind of worker under one roof before collapsing almost as quickly as it had risen.
lesson.body:
The Knights of Labor began in 1869 in Philadelphia, founded by Uriah Stephens and a small group of garment cutters. Given how badly earlier labor organizations like the National Labor Union had fared, and how readily employers blacklisted or fired known union members, the Knights initially operated as a secret society, complete with rituals and passwords, to protect its members from retaliation.

The organization changed dramatically under Terence Powderly, who became its Grand Master Workman in 1879 and dropped much of the secrecy as membership grew. By 1886, the Knights had reached a peak membership of roughly 700,000, making it by far the largest labor organization the country had yet seen. Its vision was strikingly broad for the time. Rather than organizing only skilled workers in a single trade, the Knights welcomed skilled and unskilled workers alike, including women and, in many locals, African American workers, though in the South this often meant separate, segregated local assemblies rather than true integration. The Knights pursued sweeping reforms well beyond wages: an eight hour workday, an end to child labor, and even, for some members, a vision of replacing the wage system entirely with worker owned cooperatives. Powderly himself preferred arbitration to strikes, seeing strikes as a last resort rather than a primary tool.

The Knights were not free of the prejudices of their era. Like most of the American labor movement at the time, the organization supported restricting Chinese immigration and excluded Chinese workers from membership, a position that reflected the widespread anti Chinese sentiment that culminated in the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.

The Knights' downfall came suddenly. On May 4, 1886, a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square, organized in connection with the broader movement for an eight hour day that the Knights had supported, turned deadly when someone threw a bomb into a line of police officers, killing several. In the wave of anti radical hysteria that followed, known as the Haymarket Affair, organized labor as a whole was tarred with the brush of violence and anarchism, even though the Knights of Labor had no responsibility for the bombing. Membership collapsed within a few years, falling from its 1886 peak to a small fraction of that size, worsened by a string of failed strikes and by growing tension between Powderly's cautious leadership and members who wanted more aggressive action. The organization's decline left an opening that a very different kind of labor federation, the American Federation of Labor, would fill.
